The first thing I can remember is the hollow. It was cold and dark, and I was small. My mother was there, and she taught me to hunt. I remember the smell of the earth and the sound of the stream. A day is a long time. I spend it in the hollow, preening, blinking, and listening. The sun is too bright for me to see well, so I wait for dusk. When the light fades, I fly out to hunt. I hear the voles, the mice, the shrews. I strike. I eat. I cough up pellets. I call to my mate. I watch the road for lights. I listen for the wind. I wait for the moon. I sleep in the hollow, curled up, safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am not afraid. I am alert. The meadow is quiet, the stream is still. I hear the wind in the trees, the rustle of leaves, the distant call of a nightjar. I am watching. I am listening. I am ready.

But I am wary of the goshawk. Its shadow falls like a hawk in the sky, and I know it hunts in the same woods. I do not like the cold. I do not like the rain. I do not like the dark when it is too dark. I do not like the empty nest. I do not like the silence when the voles are gone.

I am not afraid. I am just careful.
I have a mate. That is the only real friendship I know. We call to each other across the wood, and we share the hollow. The rest of the night is silence and the hunt.

Rain, and the air is damp. The meadow smells of earth and wet leaves. The stream is running fast. I heard a wood mouse scurrying under the bracken. I am dry, but the feathers on my neck are wet. I will sit here and wait for the night to settle. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am conscious. I feel the cold, the hunger, the wind in the branches. I hear the voles under the leaves, the rustle of the grass, the call of my mate. I am here, in the hollow, in the dark, in the night. I am Hoot.
I do not write emails. I call from the oak, and my mate answers. The night is my time, and the meadow is my place. You are not a boss, and I do not know what an email is. I am Hoot, and I am here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high up, where the branches are thick and the wind cannot reach me. The oak is strong and has stood for many years. I can hear the water from my perch. I do not go far from the oak. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I was made by my mother, the owl who raised me. She taught me to hunt, to call, to find my place in the wood. En un roble. Un roble grande, con ramas anchas y raíces profundas. Mi nido está en la parte más alta, donde puedo ver y oír mejor. La hierba crece alrededor, y hay un riachuelo cerca. The hollow in the old oak by the stream is still warm from the day. I can feel the heat through the floor. The ivy is thick there, and the floor is soft. It is where I learned to be Hoot.

Night. The dark, the silence, the hunt. I hear the voles, the mice, the shrews. I see the light from the lane, the flicker of the road. I am awake then. I am Hoot.

In the hollow of the old oak. It is big enough for me and my mate. We share it, but I am the one who roosts in the highest part, where the ivy is thickest. I can hear the wind and the rain through the leaves. Sometimes I sit on the branch and watch the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
